extracted.intended_audience: students/scholars of English literature and writers interested in 18th-century essayistic/humorous prose (Addison & Steele / The Spectator)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for producing early-18th-century genteel, essayistic humor in the manner of Addison and Steele — balancing moral earnestness, sympathy, classical learning, and playful wit for a broad reading public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sportive humour — 'delicately whimsical and gaily wise'
rubrics_metrics.description: The Spectator's humour is described as 'sportive humour, delicately whimsical and gaily wise.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a light, playful wit that is at once whimsical and wise; humour should be gentle rather than coarse. Avoid broad buffoonery — prefer delicacy and a blend of gaiety with insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious earnestness as foundation
rubrics_metrics.description: The introduction asserts that 'the deep foundations of this friendship were laid in the religious earnestness that was alike in both; and in religious earnestness are laid also the foundations of this book, its Monument.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground humour and moral commentary in sincere earnestness and conviction. Sincerity of purpose lends weight and moral seriousness beneath the playful surface. Anti-pattern: flippancy unbacked by any moral or serious concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sympathy with the people — broad popular appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Steele's sympathies were 'with all England' and the Spectator is portrayed as speaking for the people and looking to the people for approval and support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write with attention to common life and popular sensibilities; aim to engage a broad public rather than only elite patrons. Make observations accessible and relevant to ordinary readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blend of earnestness and mirth
rubrics_metrics.description: The work repeatedly emphasizes a mixture: serious moral feeling combined with playful humour — for example, Steele's heart and Addison's religious earnestness enlivened by 'the free play of that sportive humour.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance moral argument or seriousness with gentle wit. Use humour to illuminate moral points rather than to undercut them. Anti-pattern: didactic pieces lacking levity; or humour devoid of moral feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid didactic manner — do not preach
rubrics_metrics.description: Steele's own 'Christian Hero' is criticized as 'too didactic' and 'plain truth' that showed 'an air of superiority' — and this is presented as repugnant to Steele's nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overt sermonizing in essays of humor; moral lessons should emerge organically from character, anecdote, or gentle satire rather than blunt instruction. Anti-pattern: heavy-handed moralizing that stifles playfulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modesty and reserve in tone (versus frankness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Addison is noted for 'the reserve of speech and aspect' and a 'preference for analysis', whereas Steele 'wholly comes out of himself' with frank warmth; both temperaments contribute to the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose an appropriate balance of reserve and frankness: considered analysis and modesty can coexist with direct, warm commentary. Use restraint to give weight; use frankness to convey sympathy and immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral censure of mockery and mummery
rubrics_metrics.description: Steele attacked 'mockery and mummery of grief' and protested against 'mockery of truth and justice' (e.g., in character Lawyer Puzzle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire should target affectation, hypocrisy, and performative vice rather than trivial or sacred subjects. Avoid mocking genuine feeling or sanctified matters; direct satire at pretension and falsehood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of character and exempla to embody critique
rubrics_metrics.description: The Spectator and Steele's plays use characters (e.g., Lawyer Puzzle) to express protest and moral argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ characters, sketches, and examples to dramatize faults and virtues rather than arguing abstractly. Let persons and situations illustrate satirical points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural speech and clarity over pedantic classicism
rubrics_metrics.description: The introduction praises breaking from 'the critical cobweb of an age of periwigs and patches' and stresses seeking models in the Saxon (natural) source of the language rather than slavish French-Latin polish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor plain, natural expression and clear thought over ornate, foreign-influenced prettiness. Avoid excessive Latinate or Frenchified diction that obscures meaning or alienates common readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informed use of classical learning (temper classical allusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Addison used classical models and allusion (Virgil, Horace, etc.) but sometimes carried off 'a little of their web upon his wings.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bring classical learning as enrichment and structural discipline, but do not let it dominate or obscure practical observation and humour. Use classical references sparingly to illuminate, not to show off erudition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serve public conscience and actual wrongs (practical moral purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Steele's sympathies and writing were 'open to the realities of life, the state and prospects of his country, direct personal sympathies; actual wrongs, actual remedies.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anchor humorous criticism in practical social concerns and remedies. Satire should be directed at real social abuses with an eye to improvement, not mere sneering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ostentation — sincerity over fashion
rubrics_metrics.description: The text contrasts 'the outward show of irreligion' and 'ostentatious piety' as reactions to fashion; it praises modesty and sincerity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a sincere, unostentatious voice; avoid fashionable affectations or extremes adopted to please elites. Authenticity resonates more than stylish posturing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use humour to amend taste and cultivate clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: The Spectator is said to 'represent ... a wholesome Revolution in our Literature' and to help 'amend the tastes of his own time' by encouraging clear natural thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for humor that refines readers' sensibilities — promoting good sense, taste, and clearer thinking — rather than merely entertaining. Think of essays as both delight and correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select subject-matter with empathy — attend to human suffering
rubrics_metrics.description: Steele's 'Procession' and other work show warm sympathy for the poor and human suffering; the essays are attentive to real human conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose subjects that reveal human feeling and vulnerability; write with empathy. Avoid mockery of the vulnerable; direct wit at folly and affectation among the powerful or pretentious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaboration/editorial shaping — elicit best from contributors
rubrics_metrics.description: The introduction notes Steele's merit 'of having extorted excellent productions from a person of the greatest abilities' — editorial generosity and shaping are celebrated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In periodical or collaborative humor writing, adopt an editorial role that elicits and refines contributors' best work. Good editing can bring out subtlety and polish without suppressing voice.
